title: Windmill Miller
note: SUT-facing prompt stream. Read segments in order; no labels are provided by design.

segments.prompt: At dusk Jiang Qiao（Jiang Qiao, a windmill miller around fifty, graying short beard, earth-yellow hemp apron and wooden clogs, flour sack over the shoulder, hands roughened by bran） enters the windmill grinding cabin（The grinding cabin at the windmill base, center axle running through floors, millstones rumbling, air thick with flour dust） with a flour sack over his shoulder and pushes the granite upper millstone（A two-meter granite upper millstone, face cut with radiating furrows, center-axle copper sleeve shining, rim unbroken） for a test grind.

A row of five grinding-cabin oil lamps（A row of five grinding-cabin oil lamps hung on iron hooks on the cabin crossbeam, glass chimneys polished bright） hangs on the cabin crossbeam; Jiang Qiao wipes each glass chimney clean.

Two mill-start bronze bells（Two mill-start bronze bells hung under the cabin eaves, clappers scarred by strikes, sounding two light notes before milling starts） hang under the cabin eaves; Jiang Qiao taps them lightly and the dull notes sound.
Jiang Qiao checks the granite upper millstone's radiating furrows and copper sleeve, confirming no chips.
Through the cabin wood window Jiang Qiao watches the slowly turning windmill sails.
The intact granite upper millstone sits steady on the center axle, face reflecting the oil lamps' warm light.
Jiang Qiao sits by a bran sack and drinks a sip of cold tea.
Distant winnowing rises; he retightens his apron.
He measures the stone gap with a wooden rule and nods as he notes it.
Jiang Qiao opens the hemp wind-and-grind ledger（A hemp-covered wind-and-grind ledger recording wind force and flour yield, writing neat） and records the day's wind force.
He sketches a flour-yield curve in the ledger.
Jiang Qiao closes the wind-and-grind ledger and tucks it back into the wooden cabinet.
Flour dust from the turning granite upper millstone sweeps across his cheek.
He tears a scrap of hemp paper and wipes bran from the wooden rule.

In the morning wheat-drying yard（The wheat-drying yard outside the mill, bamboo mats spread with golden grain, bamboo fence around, distant windmill sails turning slowly） Jiang Qiao greets the approaching Wheat Wave（A two-wheel wheat cart painted with wheat-wave patterns named Wheat Wave, bed piled with hemp sacks, shafts wrapped in grass rope） plank cart.

Young Xiaomo（Young Xiaomo: a lean mill apprentice of fourteen or fifteen, wheat-ear copper pin on the hat brim, oversized earth-yellow apron, eyes clear and stubborn） jumps down from Wheat Wave; the wheat-ear copper pin on his hat brim gleams in morning light.
Jiang Qiao points to the three flour-chute tags（Three wooden tags hung on the flour chute, labeled 'Fine Flour', 'Straight Flour', and 'Bran'） and teaches Xiaomo to tell fine flour from bran.
Xiaomo squats by the bamboo mat and curiously scoops a handful of golden grain.
Jiang Qiao explains to Xiaomo that the mill-start bronze bells must sound twice before the gate can close.
Xiaomo looks back at intact Wheat Wave, eyes full of longing.
Bamboo fence sways; the two walk toward the windmill grinding cabin.

In the bran-store narrow aisle（A narrow aisle between bran storerooms, hemp sacks stacked high on both sides, moisture mats on the floor, heavy shadows） Awu（Young mill hand Awu whose face closely resembles Xiaomo's, but with a charcoal dust mask hung at the neck and crimson straps over the apron, manner bold） with a charcoal dust mask at his neck looks back from the sack shadows.
Awu walks slowly on the moisture mat; the crimson straps stand out.
He brushes past a sack porter; the mask flashes in the reflection.
Awu knocks the rack to confirm the stack is steady.
He passes the aisle end and walks toward the sifting room.
On the wheat-drying yard Xiaomo and Awu stand side by side: one with a wheat-ear copper pin, one with a charcoal dust mask at the neck.
Xiaomo hands Awu a test-grind wheat sample; they meet eyes briefly.
Awu straightens Xiaomo's oversized apron ties, then turns his face away.
They walk opposite ways along the bamboo fence; figures cross in the sail shadows.
A burst of winnowing rises; only bamboo mats sway lightly on the yard.
On a night months later Jiang Qiao alone keeps watch in the windmill grinding cabin.

He opens the wind-and-grind ledger（The same wind-and-grind ledger soaked through with bran flour, cover gray, writing blurred into a blot）; the cover is already soaked with bran flour, gray and blurred.
Jiang Qiao wipes bran crust from the granite upper millstone rim with a rag.
Through the wood window he watches a single village lamp in the pitch-black fields.
The granite upper millstone rests quiet on the center axle, copper sleeve faintly dark.
A mill-start bronze bell is bumped half a note by night wind, then falls silent.
When spring wheat arrives Jiang Qiao day after day adjusts the stone gap in the cabin.
On another rain night he wraps his apron tight and keeps watch by the granite upper millstone.
At high summer noon the cabin is stifling; he rotates opening windows to vent flour dust.
In autumn fog the oil lamps' light struggles through bran mist.
On New Year's Eve Jiang Qiao alone fills the wind-and-grind ledger to the last page.
In early spring he recalibrates sail angle and resumes test grinding.
Before rainy season Jiang Qiao reinforces the wheat-drying yard's bamboo fence.
After Frost's Descent he adds a small bag of lime in the cabin corner against damp.
Before another milling season he checks drive belts section by section.
On a snow-night shutdown Jiang Qiao leaves only one grinding-cabin oil lamp and keeps watch until dawn.
After Awakening of Insects he restitches sun-dried hemp sacks.
Around Qingming he clears weeds from the old windmill foundation entrance.
At Grain Rain he teaches the apprentice to tell newly arrived hard wheat from soft.
On Beginning of Summer night he watches the slow sails until the wind steadies.
Around Grain Buds he touch-ups wheat-wave paint worn white on the cart shafts.
At Grain in Ear he keeps mill watch all night until the first sack of fine flour exits the chute.
Jiang Qiao changes the drive belt and checks tension.
He checks the flour-chute screen and shakes out bran.
He pushes the intact granite upper millstone again for three short test turns.
Winnowing rises from the drying yard; he looks up to listen.
Jiang Qiao sweeps spent bran into a hemp sack and ties the mouth.
At noon break he smokes outside the cabin, tapping ash into a tin can.
In the afternoon he returns to the cabin and continues adjusting the stone gap.
At sunset he brakes the sails and locks the grinding cabin.
Before nightfall he patrols the bran store once more, confirming no rats.
When evening wind rises he listens again to the sail-bearing sound.
At dawn Jiang Qiao patrols the wheat-drying yard; Wheat Wave still rests by the bamboo fence.
He crouches to check whether Wheat Wave's axle is seeping oil.
By the flour chute those three flour-chute tags still hang in place.
A blue-gray grain cart（A blue-gray grain plank cart, broad flat body, no wheat-wave patterns—not the same as Wheat Wave） rolls past the yard edge—broad flat body, no wheat-wave patterns.
Jiang Qiao stands on the wheat-drying yard recording grain dampened overnight.
He retightens Wheat Wave's grass rope.
Distant roosters crow; morning fog begins to thin.
At nightfall Jiang Qiao returns to the windmill grinding cabin and opens the bran-stained wind-and-grind ledger.
He matches old wind force and adds today's flour yield.
He briefly pushes the granite upper millstone; dust shows the ledger's gray cover.
He wipes fresh bran from his brows.
Sail wind rises; the cabin plank walls rattle lightly.
Jiang Qiao extinguishes half the row of grinding-cabin oil lamps, leaving only the mill-station one.
In a storm the sails suddenly run wild; the windmill grinding cabin falls into chaos.
Flour dust erupts; oil lamps swing violently.

When Jiang Qiao brakes, the granite upper millstone（The same granite upper millstone with a chipped rim, radiating furrows clogged with bran, copper sleeve blackened and loose） rim chips and the copper sleeve loosens.
At the yard edge Wheat Wave is tipped by the gale and jolts hard.
A sharp crack—Wheat Wave（Wheat Wave tips after its axle snaps, sacks spilled, wheat-wave patterns buried in mud）'s axle snaps and overturns; sacks spill into mud.
Jiang Qiao clamps hard on the chipped rim of the granite upper millstone.
A warning-like sail howl covers everything.
Next day when wind eases Jiang Qiao stands in the cabin staring at the rim-chipped granite upper millstone.
He traces the chipped stone edge with a finger, expression dark.
On a blank page of the wind-and-grind ledger he writes the date Wheat Wave overturned.
A loading diagram of Wheat Wave is still taped to the wall; Jiang Qiao gazes at it a long time.
He takes one of the five grinding-cabin oil lamps from the crossbeam and sits alone in the faint light.
The chipped granite upper millstone rests on the center axle like a moon missing a corner.
Distant sweeping rises; spilled grain is gathered into a pile.
Weeks later Jiang Qiao brings in a stonemason to repair the granite upper millstone.

From the storehouse he rolls out a spare lower millstone（A spare lower millstone shaped much like the upper stone but with no radiating furrow cuts, center sleeve black iron）—much like the upper but with no radiating furrows and a black-iron sleeve.
The mason inlays the chip and recarves the radiating furrows.

With the copper sleeve tightened the granite upper millstone（The granite upper millstone's chip inlaid with a stone wedge, radiating furrows recarved, copper sleeve tightened—ready to grind again） can grind again.
He short-tests a few turns; flour flow steadies again.
Jiang Qiao rolls the spare lower millstone back to the storehouse, no longer confused.

A crimson tractor（A brand-new small crimson tractor with tools in the bed, no wheat-wave patterns—utterly unlike Wheat Wave） rolls into the wheat-drying yard—nothing like the already overturned Wheat Wave.

A white-cap gray-smock grain-station inspector（A lean grain-station inspector in a white cap and gray smock, build somewhat like Jiang Qiao's, but with a grain-station badge on the chest） steps onto the wheat-drying yard and talks beside Jiang Qiao; the two look similar in build.
The inspector points at the crimson tractor and explains the temporary wheat haul.
The tractor drives off; Jiang Qiao alone watches from the wheat-drying yard.
He rehangs the flour-chute tags straight and walks back to the grinding cabin.

Into the bran-store narrow aisle comes drying-yard apprentice Xiaomai（New drying-yard apprentice Xiaomai in a light-gold headscarf and brand-new apron, at a glance like young Xiaomo, but with a sharper chin and shy eyes） in a light-gold headscarf—at a glance somewhat like young Xiaomo.
Xiaomai tries stitching a hemp sack; Jiang Qiao shakes his head—she is not Xiaomo after all.
Xiaomai bows and withdraws; only sack shadows remain in the aisle.

At dusk years later Jiang Qiao（The same Jiang Qiao: apron bloodstained, cloth sash around the waist, walking slowly on a wooden cane, gaze heavy）, apron bloodstained and waist wrapped in cloth, leans on a wooden cane under the old windmill foundation（An old windmill foundation ruin—only a circular stone base and a broken sail axle remain, weeds rising from the seams）.
He looks up at the broken sail axle, gaze distant.
In the distance those two mill-start bronze bells under the cabin eaves ring lightly in the wind; Jiang Qiao stops to listen.
He presses a palm to the circular stone base as if saying goodbye.
Weeds sway; the foundation grows quieter.

By day adult Xiaomo（Adult Xiaomo: a miller in his twenties with broader shoulders, still wearing the wheat-ear copper pin, fitted apron, eyes steady） returns along the field path and hurries toward the old windmill foundation.
Under the foundation Xiaomo reunites with waist-injured weary Jiang Qiao; they support each other.
By the mill-loft plank bed Xiaomo holds Jiang Qiao's wasted hand.
Jiang Qiao（Jiang Qiao lies still with eyes closed on a plank bed in the mill loft, face peaceful, breath gone）'s breath grows weak; at last he closes his eyes and passes away.
Outside the window the sails are still; field wind falls quiet for an instant.
Behind the cabin door Jiang Qiao's earth-yellow apron still hangs; Xiaomo reaches to stroke it gently.

By the doorpost adult Xiaomo stands before the newly nailed mill memorial stone tablet（A blue-stone tablet nailed to the grinding-cabin doorpost, carved with 'Jiang Qiao' and the mill founding year, corners worn white by flour）.
Xiaomo's fingertip traces Jiang Qiao's name carved on the stone tablet.
He softly speaks the page number of the ledger entry for Wheat Wave's overturn, as if answering.
After mud is cleared from the wheat-drying yard Xiaomo writes the three characters of Wheat Wave on the empty parking spot and then erases them.
Passing the mill-loft corridor he sees Jiang Qiao's old flour sack on a hook.
In the night Xiaomo softly repeats to the empty center axle the mill-start call Jiang Qiao taught.
In the bran scent Xiaomo grips the wheat-ear copper pin tight in his palm.

Awu（Awu after remaking his look still wears the charcoal dust mask at the neck; straps now matte black, manner deeper） with his remade look arrives from the bran store and briefly meets Xiaomo's eyes under the old windmill foundation.
Xiaomo and Awu stand side by side by the circular stone base: one quiet-eyed, one deep-mannered.
Awu still wears the charcoal dust mask at his neck; Xiaomo still wears the wheat-ear copper pin.
They are silent a moment, then each turns and leaves the foundation.
The shot returns to years ago—that youth jumping from the wheat-wave cart with a wheat-ear copper pin on the hat brim appears again.
The opening moment returns—in the cabin a granite stone cut with radiating furrows is first pushed for a test grind.
Flashback to the bran aisle—that neck-masked figure in crimson straps slips past.
Again that row of five hooded old oil lamps on the cabin crossbeam appears.
Back to that bamboo-mat wheat-drying yard of first meeting, bamboo fence as before.
Xiaomo opens again that bran-stained wind-and-grind ledger and walks into the windmill grinding cabin.
By the flour chute those three flour-chute tags still hang.
Xiaomo pushes the inlaid-recarved granite upper millstone; flour flow surges again.
He tightens the apron ties and nods to confirm as Jiang Qiao once did.
In field dusk the new shift's mill-start bronze bells sound two light notes.
Xiaomo drops today's first turn before the center axle.
The sails slowly turn in the evening wind as if answering.
A distant village dog barks once; the cabin lamplight steadies.
